title: There is no theory for extrapolating successful replication of selected trials to new questions
statement: Agreement between an emulation and a randomized trial raises confidence, and disagreement can arise from emulation failure, random error, different adherence, different measurement, different populations, or a limitation of the trial itself. RCT-DUPLICATE and the 2026 concordance meta-analysis both show better agreement under closer emulation and neither shows equivalence: across 107 paired emulations and trials the effect correlation was 0.59 overall and 0.83 among the 63 pairs judged to emulate more closely. What no one has is a theory that licenses the inference from those results to a new question: how much confidence a successful replication of trial A in database D transfers to question B in database D, or to question A in database E. Publishing after the trial result is known also creates design-calibration and selective-reporting risks that the concordance statistic cannot see.
why_open: The benchmarking set is not a random sample of questions: trials get emulated when they are recent, large, and have an accessible active comparator, which are the conditions under which emulation works best. A concordance statistic is therefore an estimate of performance on a favorable subpopulation, with no design that would identify performance elsewhere. Attributing a discrepancy requires knowing which of six candidate causes produced it, and the data that would separate them, particularly the trial's own adherence and measurement, are typically not available to the emulator.

proposed_direction: Run prospective, blinded benchmarking suites in which the emulation protocol and code are frozen and registered before the trial result is revealed, which removes design calibration by construction rather than by assurance. Model concordance hierarchically by data source, clinical setting, outcome type and degree of protocol match, so the quantity estimated is a conditional expectation of agreement rather than a global rate. Treat benchmarking as calibration evidence about a data source and a design class, never as certification of a method.
severity: Benchmarking results are cited as general warrant for emulation, and the inference from them to a new question has no support.

opinions.rationale: The narrow identification concern is correct: performance on selected trial-database pairs does not nonparametrically identify performance for a new question or database without a defined target distribution, a sampling or selection model, conditional exchangeability of benchmark performance, and positivity over the relevant design and setting modifiers. The assertion that there is "no theory" or "no design" is too absolute. Transport and hierarchical prediction are possible under explicit assumptions, although a hierarchical model cannot identify extrapolation outside observed support merely by conditioning on study features. Correlation is also not an agreement measure: it can be high despite systematic bias and low because of restricted effect variation or sampling error. Freezing the protocol prospectively blocks outcome-informed design adaptation only if all analytic choices are locked; it does not by itself prevent selective reporting after unblinding. The problem remains open in its narrower form because the supplied agenda does not provide an identified and validated transfer procedure. Its very-high severity is warranted only when benchmarking is used to certify decisions beyond the benchmarked design class.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: A successful replication identifies calibration only for the evaluated trial, protocol, and database. Quantitative transfer to another question or database requires a prespecified target performance estimand, an explicit selection or transport model, conditional exchangeability, and overlap in relevant modifiers; outside that support, transfer is model-dependent rather than identified.

opinions.rationale: Inverted prior favors solutions that license transfer of successful A-in-D replications to B-in-D or A-in-E. BenchExCal (Wang et al. 2025) is exactly that transfer procedure for indication expansion: benchmark an existing-indication trial in the database, then calibrate a subsequent database study for the expanded question using the observed RCT–database differences. Kirchgesner et al. (2024) state a related trial-calibration approach for questions RCTs never answered. Heyard et al. (2024) and the BMJ 2026 concordance meta-analysis already move from a global agreement rate toward design-conditional agreement (protocol match, baseline balance, outcome quality, claims vs other sources). Prospective prediction projects (GRADE, semaglutide phase IV, FDA prediction workstream) partially remove design-calibration by freezing protocols before trial readout. None of this is a completed, general statistical theory that quantifies how much confidence transfers to arbitrary new questions or databases, and BenchExCal’s empirical evaluation is still planned (simulation plus five examples), not finished. The six-cause attribution problem for single discrepancies remains open. Saying there is “no theory” is therefore too strong; the gap is the lack of a validated general theory and completed prospective hierarchical calibration, not a blank slate.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: There is no validated, general theory that licenses quantitative transfer of confidence from successful replications of selected favorable trials to arbitrary new questions or databases; proposed frameworks (BenchExCal, trial calibration) and design-conditional concordance analyses exist but are incomplete or unevaluated for that licensing role.

resolving_work.title: A Benchmark, Expand, and Calibration (BenchExCal) Trial Emulation Approach for Using Real-World Evidence to Support Indication Expansions: Design and Process for a Planned Empirical Evaluation
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Proposes an operational theory for transferring a successful existing-indication emulation (question A in database D) into a calibrated second-stage emulation for an expanded indication (question B in D), with simulation and five planned empirical evaluations. Directly addresses the report’s missing transfer step, though as proposal plus planned evaluation rather than finished validation.
resolving_work.quote: Confidence in the validity of findings from cohort studies conducted using databases (hereafter "database study") to support indication expansions could be increased through a structured benchmarking process of an initial database study against RCT evidence followed by calibration of a subsequent database study based on differences in results observed in the initial RCT-database pair. This paper proposes a benchmark, expand, and calibration (BenchExCal) approach to trial emulation and describes the design and process for evaluating the performance of the approach through both simulation studies; five planned empirical examples are also described.

resolving_work.quote: Among 107 target trial emulation-randomised controlled trial pairs, the Pearson correlation coefficient was 0.59 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.45 to 0.70), standardised difference agreement was 79% (85/107), and summary ratio of ratios was 0.96 (95% CI 0.92 to 1.01; I2=36%). opinions.rationale: The claim is internally consistent and proportionate. It correctly identifies a structural gap: existing benchmarking provides empirical concordance on a favorable subpopulation but lacks a formal theory for extrapolating this to new questions or databases. The reasons given (non-random sampling of trials, multiple confounding causes for discrepancies) directly support why the problem remains open. The claim is appropriately scoped as a limitation of current methodological frameworks rather than an impossibility.

title: Replication is reported as a binary label rather than as a calibrated comparison of estimands
statement: Agreement between an emulation and a trial is informative only when the estimands, populations and measurements are close enough to be comparable, and better design alignment is empirically associated with stronger concordance. Benchmarking nonetheless reports success or failure as a binary label, usually derived from whether the confidence intervals overlap or whether the direction agrees. That label mixes estimand mismatch with random error: two studies estimating the same quantity with wide intervals will agree by that criterion, and two estimating different quantities precisely will disagree. The reported statistic therefore does not measure what its users take it to measure.
why_open: Constructing a graded measure requires deciding how much estimand difference is tolerable, which is a judgment the binary label exists to avoid. Prediction-interval coverage would be the natural criterion and requires a distributional claim about the trial's own error that the trial does not publish. The label is also convenient for the audiences who cite benchmarking results, so there is little pressure to replace it.

proposed_direction: Report the ratio of effects, the absolute effect difference, standardized agreement and prediction-interval coverage together, so that estimand mismatch and random error are separately visible. Use positive and negative controls alongside the trial comparison, and prefer prospective forecasts of a trial's result to retrospective comparisons, since only the former is uncontaminated by knowing the answer. Replicate across databases as well as across questions, because a data source's calibration is what a decision-maker actually needs to know.
severity: The binary label is what gets cited, and it conflates the two things a reader needs to separate.

opinions.rationale: The entry criticizes binary replication labels. The concordance meta-analysis it draws on does not use one: it reports correlation and standardized-difference agreement and relates them to design features, which is the graded reporting the entry asks for. RCT-DUPLICATE similarly reports several agreement metrics. So the criticism lands on the citing practice rather than on the benchmarking literature, and the entry should say that. The part that survives is that a graded criterion still does not separate estimand mismatch from random error, since prediction-interval coverage requires a distributional claim about the trial's own error that trials do not publish.

opinions.rationale: The criticism of confidence-interval overlap and sign agreement is technically sound, but the problem is framed too broadly. The agenda's own descriptions say that the cited benchmarks already report several graded metrics, including effect correlation and standardized differences, so benchmarking is not uniformly binary. Continuous effect differences, ratios, and standardized contrasts still cannot separate estimand mismatch from random error. That separation first requires commensurate estimands and then a joint sampling model incorporating uncertainty from both estimates, their covariance when applicable, and between-pair heterogeneity. Prediction-interval coverage does not require a trial to publish a full error distribution when an estimate and standard error or confidence interval are available, and coverage is itself calibrated across a suite rather than diagnosed from one pair. Ratios are additionally unstable when the reference effect is near zero. This is therefore partly an implementation and reporting problem with existing tools, not wholly an unresolved statistical-method problem; high severity is disproportionate unless the binary label is the sole basis for a decision.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Binary replication labels based on interval overlap or effect direction discard magnitude and uncertainty and cannot diagnose why estimates differ. Decision-grade benchmarking should first align estimands, then report paired contrasts with joint uncertainty, heterogeneity, and prespecified tolerances whenever a categorical judgment is required.

opinions.rationale: The claim that benchmarking “nonetheless reports success or failure as a binary label” is not faithful to the field’s primary programs or to the report’s own cited works. RCT-DUPLICATE and Franklin-line methods report regulatory/significance agreement, estimate agreement, and standardized-difference agreement together; the BMJ 2026 meta-analysis leads with Pearson correlation, ICC, ratio of ratios, standardized-difference agreement, and Bland–Altman, and only secondarily with binary metrics. Köppe, Micheloud, Erdmann, Heyard, and Held (2025) go further: they replace the two-trials (regulatory agreement) rule with the graded sceptical p-value, which uses both p-values, effect sizes, and relative precision, and invert it to combined confidence intervals; they apply it to 29 RCT-DUPLICATE pairs. ISPOR Europe 2024 also floated enhanced multi-metric RCT–RWE agreement assessments for HTA. What remains open is universal adoption, explicit estimand alignment (how much estimand difference is tolerable), and routine prediction-interval coverage that treats trial sampling error as a distribution. Binary labels are still convenient for secondary citation and still appear beside continuous metrics, but they are not the sole or best existing practice. The report’s proposed direction (ratio of effects, absolute difference, standardized agreement, prediction-interval coverage, prospective forecasts) is largely what the better literature already does or is building.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Binary agreement labels remain common in secondary reporting of benchmarking and are still listed among primary metrics, even though leading programs and the 2026 concordance meta-analysis already report continuous multi-metric comparisons; a fully estimand-calibrated prediction-interval criterion that cleanly separates estimand mismatch from random error is not yet standard.

resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Primary reporting is continuous and multi-metric (correlation 0.59/0.83, ratio of ratios, standardized-difference rates, design-feature regressions), not a binary success label. Directly undercuts the claim that benchmarking only reports binary agreement.
resolving_work.quote: Most target trial emulation-randomised controlled trial pairs met one or more of the binary agreement metrics for concordance (table 3): standardised difference agreement (85/107; 79%), estimate agreement (82/107; 77%), full agreement for statistical significance (53/107; 50%), and partial agreement for statistical significance (20/41; 49%). The Pearson coefficient between target trial emulation-randomised controlled trial pairs was 0.59 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.45 to 0.70), and the intraclass correlation coefficient was 0.56 (95% CI 0.42 to 0.68), consistent with moderate correlation.

[...] The sceptical p-value can be interpreted quantitatively: Smaller pS values indicate a higher degree of replication success. counter_evidence.quote: Previously published literature applied the three statistical metrics used in this study to evaluate the success of the emulation. However, these metrics alone are not sufficient to determine if an emulation has been successful, as each has their limitations. Both estimate agreement and standardized difference agreement fail to incorporate the uncertainty that comes with the target trial estimate. [...] Moreover, statistical significance agreement is disproportionately harsh when estimates (or their CI limits) lay close to the null.

opinions.rationale: The claim is internally consistent and proportionate. It accurately characterizes a limitation in current practice: benchmarking often relies on binary labels (e.g., CI overlap) that conflate estimand mismatch with random error. The stated reasons for it being open (the difficulty of defining tolerable estimand differences and the convenience of binary labels) logically support the persistence of this practice. The claim is appropriately scoped as a critique of current reporting standards rather than an impossibility claim.

title: Data-fitness assessment is narrative and has no thresholds that would stop a study
statement: Electronic health records arise from encounters, billing and documentation rather than from scheduled research assessments, so eligibility and follow-up in an emulation partly reflect care-seeking and access rather than the biology the protocol intends. Whether a given database can support a given target trial is therefore a question about the data source and the trial jointly. In practice this is answered narratively, in a paragraph asserting that the data are suitable, with no quantitative thresholds and no procedure that could return the answer no. A pipeline that cannot conclude that the trial is not emulable will always produce an estimate, and the estimate will not carry the fact that the question could not be asked.
why_open: Fitness is not a property of the data alone but of the pair formed by the data and the protocol, so a fixed score is the wrong object and a per-protocol assessment has to be constructed each time. Any threshold that would stop a study is a threshold that costs someone a publication, and no external body currently imposes one. There is also a measurement problem underneath: assessing capture continuity or outcome validity generally requires a validation source, and if that source existed the fitness question would be less pressing.

proposed_direction: Build trial-component fitness scores for observability, temporal precision, capture continuity, comparator support, outcome validity and linkage completeness, each computed against the specific protocol rather than the database in the abstract. Predefine stop rules that trigger when an essential component fails, and publish the fitness report whether or not the study proceeds, so that a negative fitness assessment is a citable result rather than a private decision. Validate the scores against benchmarking data by checking whether low fitness predicts poor concordance with the corresponding trial.
severity: A study that should never have run is indistinguishable in print from one that should.

opinions.rationale: The residual problem is real: data fitness is specific to the protocol, estimand, and decision context, and prespecified component-level no-go criteria would improve study governance. The statement nevertheless overstates the absence of quantitative assessment. Availability, temporal resolution, treatment support, follow-up continuity, outcome capture, and validation performance can all be measured, although they do not collapse into a universally valid score. External validation data are not required for every fitness component. A pipeline without explicit stop rules also does not necessarily always return an estimate, while an estimator's standard error generally will not represent bias from nonidentification or poor measurement. Benchmark concordance cannot by itself validate a fitness score because disagreement can arise from estimand differences, transportability, adherence, measurement, or bias in either study. This is decision-critical when an essential protocol component is unobservable or unsupported; otherwise, standardized scoring and publication of assessments are primarily governance and reproducibility improvements.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Many target-trial emulations lack prespecified, protocol-specific quantitative adequacy criteria and no-go rules. Transparent component-level assessments could improve decisions about whether to proceed, but thresholds must be estimand- and decision-specific, and randomized-trial concordance alone cannot validate them.

opinions.rationale: Inverted-prior search finds substantial prior art that already structures protocol-paired data fitness and can return no, so the claim that fitness is only a narrative paragraph with no thresholds and no procedure that can stop a study is overstated. SPIFD (2021) and SPIFD2 (2023) are step-by-step feasibility frameworks that pair research question, target-trial articulation, and data-source selection, with component-level documentation and heatmaps intended to support go or no-go decisions before estimation. The CARE oncology work (Levy et al., 2026) runs a systematic multi-stage fitness screen over six commercial EHR sources and 23 candidate RCTs: of 54 RCT-RWD combinations, nine reached detailed feasibility and only three were selected for emulation protocol development, with explicit fitness constraints (complex eligibility, biomarkers, performance status, outcome ascertainment). OHDSI DataQualityDashboard implements quantitative pass/fail thresholds on CDM conformance, and DARWIN EU study phases include a feasibility assessment that issues a recommendation on whether to conduct the study. Lee et al. (2026) quantifies TTE-relevant completeness, accuracy, plausibility, and concordance for an EHR cohort against Medicare claims, and Wang et al. (2026) formalizes when EHR realization of trial components can or cannot yield interpretable estimates. What remains open is exactly the hard part of the proposed agenda: field-standard, protocol-component fitness scores with pre-specified stop rules that academic pipelines cannot bypass; routine publication of negative fitness assessments as citable results; and empirical validation that low fitness predicts poor concordance with the corresponding trial. Regulatory and industry pathways already gate more often than the report implies; general-purpose TTE software (TrialEmulation and related packages) still does not enforce a fitness gate that returns no.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Outside tightly gated regulatory or network feasibility processes, many published target trial emulations still assert data suitability narratively, and there is no field-standard, protocol-component fitness score with pre-specified stop rules that is routinely published when it fails and has been validated against trial concordance.

title: An unrecorded eligibility criterion is indistinguishable from a criterion that was met
statement: Trial eligibility is assessed at a screening visit; a database records what a clinician happened to order. Restricting an emulation to patients with complete eligibility information therefore selects on laboratory testing, clinical documentation and specialist access, which differ systematically from the excluded patients. Weighting methods for missing eligibility have recently been developed and the literature remains small. The harder version of the problem is that eligibility is latent rather than merely missing: an absent creatinine value is consistent both with a patient who would have failed the criterion and with one who was never tested, and the missingness itself may depend on treatment anticipation or on the impending outcome.
why_open: Missing-at-random conditional on the recorded history is not credible here, because the recording decision is a clinical judgment informed by exactly the severity that predicts the outcome. Distinguishing latent eligibility from missing measurement requires a validation source in which the criterion was assessed for everyone, and such sources are rare and rarely representative. Imputing the value and imputing eligibility are different operations with different targets, and the literature has not separated them.

prior_work.what_it_does: Develops weighting for missing eligibility information in emulated trials, the first direct treatment of the problem.

prior_work.what_it_does: Sets out how each protocol component, eligibility included, is realized against record-level data and where the realization is partial.

proposed_direction: Model true eligibility and its observation jointly, using validation records where a criterion was assessed for everyone to anchor the measurement model. Compare multiple imputation, inverse-probability-of-eligibility weighting, doubly robust selection correction and partial-identification bounds on the same data, since they make different assumptions and currently no one knows which are tolerable. Report the eligible population under each approach alongside the effect estimate, because a method that changes who is in the trial has changed the estimand and should be read that way.
severity: Complete-case eligibility is the default in applied emulation and it selects on care intensity.

opinions.rationale: The entry says the literature on missing eligibility is small. It is small and it is larger than the one paper the entry cites. A 2026 Statistics in Medicine paper treats missingness in eligibility criteria for target trial emulation in electronic health records with survival outcomes, alongside the 2025 American Journal of Epidemiology weighting paper the entry already carries. opinions.rationale: Restricting analysis to records with observed eligibility can cause selection bias, but systematic differences between included and excluded patients do not alone establish bias for a specified causal estimand. Identification depends on conditional exchangeability for the observation or selection process and adequate observed support. When true eligibility is missing not at random, the effect among truly eligible patients is generally not identified from the main data alone. However, assessing the criterion for everyone in a validation source is sufficient, not necessary. A probability validation subsample, auxiliary-variable restrictions, explicit parametric assumptions, sensitivity analysis, or partial-identification methods can also inform the problem. If eligibility is a deterministic threshold of an underlying measurement, imputing that measurement and deriving eligibility can target the same population as directly imputing eligibility. Changing imputed membership across draws represents missing-data uncertainty and does not automatically change the estimand. Existing weighting work addresses an important identified-assumption case, while the unrestricted latent-eligibility problem remains open.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Complete-case eligibility restriction can bias an emulation when observation of the criterion depends on treatment or outcome determinants not adequately controlled in the recorded history. If true eligibility among unobserved records is missing not at random, the effect in the truly eligible population requires additional identifying assumptions or external information. Validation data are one useful source of such information, and imputing the underlying measurement versus the eligibility indicator requires different models even though coherent implementations can target the same causal estimand.

resolving_work.title: Adjusting for selection bias due to missing eligibility criteria in emulated target trials
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Provides a weighting approach for selection arising from missing eligibility information under identifying assumptions; it does not nonparametrically identify unrestricted missing-not-at-random latent eligibility.

opinions.rationale: Inverted prior: treat missing-eligibility selection as already handled, then check what exists. Three direct method papers (not one) address the complete-case selection problem under explicit missingness models. Tompsett et al. (2023) formalize bias from missing eligibility in a point-treatment TTE, show patterns under MAR and MNAR, and evaluate multiple imputation of the eligibility-defining variables plus MNAR sensitivity shifts; they state that MNAR imputation remains exploratory because the sensitivity parameters are not identified from the data alone. Benz et al. (2025; also arXiv:2406.16830), which the entry cites as the first direct treatment, develops inverse-probability-of-ascertainment weights for sequential TTE with time-to-event endpoints under an eligibility-MAR assumption (ascertainment independent of true eligibility given non-eligibility covariates and treatment), evaluates them in plasmode EHR simulations, and applies them to a Kaiser Permanente bariatric-surgery cohort; accompanying research code is on GitHub (lbenz730/missing_eligibility_tte), not a production CRAN/Python package. Shen et al. (2026, Stat Med) compares complete-case analysis with three multiple-imputation strategies for eligibility-defining variables in EHR survival TTEs and reports that flexible MI often reduces bias when missingness is high. Wang et al. (2026) map eligibility realization in EHR data and cite Tompsett and Benz as the handling literature; they do not add a new estimator. What remains open, and matches the entry’s harder claim, is latent eligibility: an absent lab is consistent with never-tested versus would-have-failed, with recording driven by the same severity that predicts treatment and outcome (MNAR not cured by MAR IPW or standard MI). No paper retrieved jointly models true eligibility and its observation process anchored to a validation source where the criterion was assessed for everyone; no head-to-head of MI, IPW, doubly robust selection correction, and partial-identification bounds on the same TTE data with reporting of the implied eligible population under each method was found. Package search (TrialEmulation, WeightIt missing-covariate handling, gfoRmula, lmtp, ltmle, zEpid, causallib) shows no shipped inverse-probability-of-eligibility-ascertainment or joint latent-eligibility measurement model. 2025–2026 guidance (TARGET, FDA RWE/ECT, EMA registry, NICE RWE) does not resolve identification of latent eligibility. Partial solve covers MAR complete-case selection; the title problem (unrecorded criterion indistinguishable from met criterion) stays open.

title: A hazard ratio is reported where the estimand was a weighted per-protocol effect among the grace-period compatible
statement: Hazard ratios, odds ratios and model coefficients are routinely presented without naming the intervention, the population, the time horizon or the strategy for each intercurrent event. ICH E9(R1) and the TARGET statement both require that objectives, estimands and sensitivity analyses be aligned, and applied reporting has not caught up. The concrete failure is specific rather than general: a reader sees a hazard ratio and infers an intention-to-treat contrast, while the analysis in fact estimated a per-protocol effect, weighted for informative censoring, among the subset of patients whose observed treatment stayed compatible with a strategy during a grace period. Those are different quantities in different populations and nothing in the presentation distinguishes them.
why_open: The hazard ratio is a familiar output that survives every methodological upgrade beneath it, so improvements in the estimator do not change what gets read. Stating the estimand precisely requires naming the population induced by cloning and censoring, which has no simple clinical description. Absolute risks and restricted mean survival differences communicate better and require the analyst to commit to a time horizon, which is an additional decision most would rather not defend.

prior_work.what_it_does: Defines the estimand attributes, population, treatment, endpoint, intercurrent-event strategy and summary measure, that an emulation report would have to fill in.

prior_work.what_it_does: A 21-item checklist requiring the target protocol and its emulation to be reported, aimed at transparency rather than at risk-of-bias certification.

proposed_direction: Require a one-sentence estimand statement naming the intervention, the population, the horizon and the intercurrent-event strategy, positioned before any effect measure. Report absolute risks, risk differences and restricted mean outcomes at clinically meaningful horizons, with the hazard ratio as a supplement rather than the headline. Include a timeline diagram showing treatment paths and censoring rules, since the population induced by cloning is easier to draw than to describe.
severity: Readers act on a quantity other than the one estimated, and the gap is systematic rather than occasional.

opinions.rationale: The estimand vocabulary is arriving in the emulation literature: a 2026 Trials paper applies a hypothetical strategy to the intercurrent event of non-adherence using the parametric g-formula, which is the ICH E9(R1) discipline executed inside a longitudinal analysis, and a 2026 Journal of Epidemiology paper argues explicitly for going beyond the hazard ratio when censoring, confounding and competing events are present. The entry's claim is about what published reports lead with rather than what is possible, and no reporting requirement in the corpus mandates a one-sentence estimand statement or absolute-risk reporting. The presence of these papers means the entry should not imply the vocabulary is missing.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Estimand vocabulary and absolute-risk alternatives are available and are being used in methodological work; no reporting standard requires an emulation to state its estimand in one sentence or to lead with an absolute measure, and hazard ratios remain the headline.

resolving_work.title: Applying a hypothetical strategy to the intercurrent event of non-adherence with the parametric g-formula
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Executes an ICH E9(R1) intercurrent-event strategy inside a g-formula analysis, which is the alignment the entry asks for.

resolving_work.title: Beyond the hazard ratio: causal inference from time-to-event data with dependent censoring, confounding, and competing events
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Argues directly against the hazard ratio as the reported quantity in this setting.

opinions.rationale: The reporting concern is valid, but the stated population is wrong. Correct clone-censor weighting does not target only patients whose observed treatment remained compatible. It reweights uncensored clone-time observations to represent artificially censored observations, thereby targeting the baseline eligible population under the specified strategies, subject to exchangeability and positivity. A bare hazard ratio identifies neither an intention-to-treat nor a per-protocol strategy and may lack a causal interpretation altogether. TARGET supplies much of the reporting solution; the residual issue is adoption rather than an unresolved estimand method.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Clone-censor-weight analyses with a grace period can estimate a marginal contrast between prespecified treatment strategies in the baseline eligible population when the artificial-censoring weights and identifying assumptions are valid; when censoring enforces adherence, the contrast is per-protocol. A bare hazard ratio does not disclose the intervention, strategy, population, follow-up horizon, or intercurrent-event handling and can therefore be misread as an intention-to-treat contrast.

resolving_work.title: Transparent Reporting of Observational Studies Emulating a Target Trial: The TARGET Statement
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Provides an explicit reporting framework for the target protocol, its emulation, and effect estimates. This resolves much of the standards gap but not compliance or the incorrect subset interpretation.

counter_evidence.quote: uncensored observations are up-weighted to represent censored observations with similar characteristics and thus to allow unbiased estimation of the causal effect of interest.
the hazard ratio (HR) cannot have a causal interpretation, as it is an average of conditional time-specific effects from a cohort changing over time.

opinions.rationale: The problem is framed as a presentation/practice failure after standards already exist: a reader sees a bare hazard ratio and infers an intention-to-treat contrast, while the analysis estimated a censoring-weighted per-protocol effect among grace-period–compatible (often cloned) patients. Maringe et al. (IJE 2020; 10.1093/ije/dyaa057), already cited, already makes the CCW estimand type explicit; that formalizes the distinction and does not change what applied papers headline. ICH E9(R1) and the TARGET statement (JAMA 2025; 10.1001/jama.2025.13350) require aligned objectives, estimands, and sensitivity analyses; TARGET item structure places target-trial protocol/estimand items (6a–g) beside emulation mapping (7a–g), and item 13 asks for effect estimates with precision including both absolute and relative measures when applicable. Official TARGET resources confirm that scope and provide protocol table and flow-diagram templates. That is real progress on the reporting-standard side and is the caveat on support: the claim is still true about practice, but “standards are missing” would be overstated after TARGET 2025. What remains open is exactly what the report names: applied reporting has not caught up; the HR remains a familiar default that survives estimator upgrades; and nothing forces a one-sentence estimand that names intervention, population induced by cloning/censoring, horizon, and intercurrent-event strategy before the first effect measure. Fourati et al. (Eur J Prev Cardiol 2026 advance article) still notes that relative measures such as hazard ratios are frequently reported and that absolute risks and risk differences at meaningful times communicate better, which is consistent with ongoing practice lag months after TARGET. title: Identification of dynamic regimes in continuous time under treatment-dependent observation is unresolved
statement: Treatments, outcomes and clinical observations occur asynchronously and are recorded at times determined by the care process. Almost every applied g-method assumes a prespecified discrete grid, and discretization can reverse temporal ordering between a treatment and an outcome that fell in the same interval, merge multiple events into one, or define an estimand that exists only relative to the chosen interval. General identification results for dynamic regimes under irregular observation, treatment-dependent visiting and within-interval effects remain limited, so the applied analyst working in continuous time has a modeling apparatus without an identification theorem to sit under it.
why_open: In continuous time the treatment process, the visit process and the outcome process are counting processes whose intensities depend on each other, and sequential exchangeability has to be stated with respect to filtrations rather than to a fixed sequence of covariate vectors. The conditions under which a dynamic regime is identified in that setting are strictly stronger and harder to interpret than their discrete counterparts. There is also no natural sample-size asymptotics: the information about an intensity comes from event counts rather than from patients, so the usual scaling arguments do not apply cleanly.

State the identification conditions in filtration terms and show which of them a standard electronic health record violates.
severity: The discretization is universal and the conditions under which it is harmless are not known.

opinions.rationale: The difficult open component is identification and estimation under explicitly defined full-data and observation-process assumptions, not a wholesale absence of continuous-time identification theory. Treatment-dependent visiting does not by itself destroy identification; the analyst must specify assumptions linking the latent longitudinal process to what is observed, together with treatment, observation and censoring positivity. If clinically relevant covariate history between visits is unobserved and no coarsening or observation model is imposed, the regime effect is generally not identified. Filtration-based exchangeability is different from, but not automatically strictly stronger than, every discrete-time formulation. Coarsening can erase or impose an incorrect ordering, although it does not mechanically reverse ordering in every shared interval. The claim that there is no natural sample-size asymptotics is false: independent patients provide a standard n-to-infinity sequence, and counting-process estimators use martingale asymptotics, with information also affected by event counts and follow-up. Grid refinement is a sensitivity analysis, not an identification test; instability does not localize a unique failure, and stability cannot validate exchangeability or the observation model.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Discretizing asynchronous clinical processes can obscure temporal ordering and change the intervention being estimated. A continuous-time emulation must define treatment, covariate, visit, censoring and outcome processes relative to a filtration and impose assumptions connecting latent histories to the observed visit process. Grid-refinement analyses can reveal sensitivity to discretization, but they cannot establish identification.

opinions.rationale: The claim that continuous-time dynamic-regime identification under irregular, process-driven observation is essentially without an identification theorem is stronger than the literature allows. Rytgaard, Gerds, and van der Laan (Annals of Statistics 2022) give a continuous-time counting-process TMLE for intervention-specific means when treatment, covariates, and outcomes occur at subject-specific times; intensities track monitoring; dynamic regimes on treatment assigned are defined with visit times kept as they naturally occur; and identification is via continuous-time g-computation under sequential exchangeability and positivity on the product-integral likelihood. Røysland, Ryalen, Nygård, and Didelez (JRSS-B 2025; arXiv:2202.02311) supply nonparametric graphical identification criteria for marginal effects of interventions on treatment-process intensities in continuous-time survival and event-history models, including structural conditions on censoring beyond classical independent censoring. Earlier continuous-time MSM and structural nested model work (Røysland; Ryalen et al. on prostate cancer) already stated filtration-based sequential exchangeability. What remains open, and why this is only partial: applied g-methods still default to discrete grids (Tankpinou et al. arXiv:2603.15924 still treats time partitioning as a consequential modeling choice); Rytgaard's main identification path intervenes on treatment decisions while leaving the visit intensity natural, so full dynamic control of a treatment-dependent informative visit process plus within-interval effects is not a closed applied recipe for EHR; software for continuous-time LTMLE is not yet a routine TTE default. Proposal papers that add unmeasured confounding (for example arXiv:2604.00544) are not resolutions. Identification theory exists; the residual gap is completeness for treatment-dependent observation, within-interval estimands, and routine practice.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Continuous-time identification and efficient estimation results for dynamic interventions under counting-process filtrations and irregular monitoring exist (Rytgaard et al. 2022; Røysland et al. 2025), but they do not yet fully settle treatment-dependent informative visit processes with within-interval effects as a default applied apparatus, and most emulations still discretize time without an identification theorem tied to the chosen grid.

title: Large databases yield small effective samples after eligibility, comparator restriction and weighting
statement: A database of millions can carry very little information about a specific target trial once strict eligibility, active-comparator restriction and weighting have been applied, and extreme weights reduce the effective sample size much further than the nominal count suggests. Conventional asymptotic inference then becomes unreliable, most sharply for rare competing events and for subgroup effects, which are precisely the quantities decision-makers ask about. Papers continue to report the nominal number of patients, which for a weighted longitudinal analysis is not the quantity that governs the variance.
why_open: The effective sample size is estimator-specific and time-varying in a longitudinal analysis, so there is no single number to report and no convention for which to choose. Small-sample corrections in this setting have to account for the estimated weights as well as the outcome model, and that theory is thin. There is also no incentive to report a number that shrinks a study's apparent size by an order of magnitude.

prior_work.cite: Robins JM, Hernán MA, Brumback B. Marginal structural models and causal inference in epidemiology. Epidemiology 2000;11(5):550-560
prior_work.what_it_does: Introduces the weighted estimator whose variance is governed by the weight distribution rather than by the record count.

prior_work.cite: lmtp: Non-Parametric Causal Effects of Feasible Interventions Based on Modified Treatment Policies. CRAN
prior_work.what_it_does: Targets shifted rather than deterministic interventions, which is one of the routes to keeping the effective sample size usable.

proposed_direction: Investigate Bayesian hierarchical g-computation, targeted shrinkage, exact or permutation-based inference, outcome-adaptive case-control sampling and cross-site borrowing for the regime where the effective sample is small. Require that the effective sample size be reported alongside the nominal one at each follow-up time, so a reader sees the information actually available. Establish by simulation the point at which asymptotic intervals stop covering, as a function of the weight tail and the event rate, so the reporting threshold is empirical rather than conventional.
severity: Nominal size is what gets reported and effective size is what determines whether the interval means anything.

opinions.rationale: Nothing in the corpus reports the effective sample size alongside the nominal one as a convention, nor establishes the point at which asymptotic intervals stop covering as a function of weight tail and event rate. Work on near-positivity violations in IPTW-estimated marginal structural survival models measures the consequence, which is the closest existing treatment, and it characterizes bias rather than supplying a reporting rule. The claim is a reporting and small-sample-inference gap rather than a missing estimator, which makes it harder to refute by finding a method paper and easier to confirm by observing practice.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Effective sample size after eligibility restriction and weighting is not conventionally reported alongside the nominal count, and no empirical threshold exists for when asymptotic inference stops covering in this setting.

resolving_work.title: Impact of near-positivity violations on IPTW-estimated marginal structural survival models with time-dependent covariates
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Quantifies the consequence of near-positivity for weighted survival estimation, which is the mechanism by which effective sample size collapses.

opinions.rationale: The central claim is correct. Eligibility and comparator restrictions reduce the number of relevant independent patients, while concentrated positive weights reduce the Kish effective sample size through (sum w)^2 divided by sum(w^2). Rare events and subgroup restrictions can leave little information despite a large source database. The important caveat is that a weight-only effective sample size is not the information governing every estimator. In longitudinal emulations it is time-specific and must account for risk sets, events, repeated or cloned records, within-patient dependence, estimated nuisance functions and the outcome variance. A small calculated effective sample size therefore does not automatically invalidate asymptotic inference; validity also depends on independent-cluster counts, event counts, weight-tail moments and nuisance-estimation behavior. Reporting time-specific weight concentration is useful but cannot replace at-risk counts, event counts, overlap plots and influence-function or cluster-level variance diagnostics. Exact or permutation inference is not generally available in observational data without a known assignment mechanism. Shrinkage and cross-site borrowing add assumptions and cannot repair structural positivity failure or absent outcome information. Simulation can characterize a specified design but cannot produce a universal coverage threshold. The lmtp software claim is unverified because no pinned lmtp source is vendored.

The core claim survives: after eligibility, active-comparator restriction, and inverse-probability weighting, information can collapse far below the nominal N, and papers still lead with headcount rather than information. What exists does not close the agenda item. Kish-style ESS, WeightIt::ESS, and cobalt balance tables already report weight-based effective sample size (including longitudinal MSM balance displays); Zhang, Bujkiewicz, and Jackson (BMC Medical Research Methodology 2024; 10.1186/s12874-024-02412-1) add three ESS estimators aimed at population-adjusted indirect comparison and general weighted analyses. Those are diagnostics for precision loss, not small-sample inference for estimated longitudinal weights plus outcome models, not time-varying ESS conventions for MSM/LTMLE follow-up, and not a simulation standard for when asymptotic intervals stop covering as a function of weight tails and event rates. lmtp's modified treatment policies help keep positivity usable but do not solve ESS reporting or finite-sample theory. No 2024 to 2026 reporting guideline (TARGET 2025, HARPER, STaRT-RWE, ENCePP) was found that requires ESS alongside nominal N at each follow-up time. Searches: effective sample size inverse probability weights MSM longitudinal 2024 2025; Zhang Bujkiewicz Jackson ESS; WeightIt ESS cobalt; small sample inference IPW MSM sandwich correction; TARGET ESS reporting. Vote open because the agenda's open parts (estimator-specific time-varying ESS convention, weight-aware small-sample theory, reporting incentive) remain; partial software and population-adjustment ESS papers are caveats, not solutions.

The claim is well-constructed and proportionate. It describes a real statistical phenomenon (effective sample size collapse under weighting and restriction) and a real reporting gap (papers report nominal counts). The reason given for openness is practical and theoretical: effective sample size is estimator-specific and time-varying so there is no single number, small-sample correction theory for estimated weights is thin, and there is no incentive to report a smaller number. None of these are impossibility claims; they are claims about the absence of convention and theory. The scope is right—it does not claim all large databases are uninformative, only that they can be, and that the reporting does not reflect the information actually available.

title: Flexible estimation is presented as a remedy for identification failure
statement: Identification is a property of the observed data together with the assumptions, not a property of the estimator. A neural network cannot learn a counterfactual contrast that the data and assumptions do not identify, and flexible modeling that reduces approximation error in a nuisance function can at the same time disguise unsupported extrapolation, because a smooth fit extends confidently into regions with no observations. The distinction is stated clearly in the methodological literature and is repeatedly elided in applied work, where a more flexible learner is offered as the answer to a confounding or positivity concern. There is no diagnostic in common use that separates a flexible model interpolating where data exist from the same model extrapolating where they do not.
why_open: Extrapolation is not visible in any conventional fit statistic: a model can have excellent cross-validated loss on the observed region and be entirely unconstrained off it. The regions that matter are conditional on a growing treatment and covariate history, so the question of whether a given prediction is supported is itself high-dimensional. The professional incentive also points one way, since the flexible estimate is the one with the tighter interval.

prior_work.cite: Feuerriegel S, Frauen D, Melnychuk V, et al. Causal machine learning for predicting treatment outcomes. Nat Med 2024;30:958-968
prior_work.what_it_does: States that causal machine learning supports individualized effect estimation only under the same identification assumptions as conventional methods, which is the claim applied work elides.

prior_work.cite: Target trial emulation under nonmutually exclusive assignment. Am J Epidemiol 2026;195(4):1045
prior_work.what_it_does: Demonstrates empirically that poor overlap defeats advanced adjustment, which is the concrete form the general point takes.

proposed_direction: Require that any flexible nuisance model be paired with a support diagnostic reported for the same conditioning sets the model uses, so extrapolation is visible where it happens rather than aggregated away. Score estimators on failure awareness: whether their diagnostics correctly signal a severe positivity violation or a non-identifiable target, tested against deliberately non-identifiable simulation scenarios. Include at least one such scenario in every methods comparison, since an estimator that always returns a narrow interval is not robust if it never warns.
severity: The confusion licenses precise answers to questions the data cannot answer, and it is spreading with the tooling.

resolving_work.title: Estimate time-varying exposure effects via ensemble learning-based marginal structural model
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Applies ensemble learning to the weight model in a longitudinal setting, which is where the extrapolation concern applies.

opinions.rationale: The central identification claim is correct, although identification formally concerns the observed-data law, causal model, target estimand, and identifying assumptions rather than the realized finite dataset. Flexible estimation cannot repair failed exchangeability or positivity. The absolute diagnostic claim is too strong: propensity-score overlap, conditional treatment probabilities, density ratios, nearest-neighbor distances, leverage, and related support diagnostics can operationally flag extrapolation. They cannot certify identification, diagnose unmeasured confounding, or provide a model-free boundary between interpolation and extrapolation in high-dimensional longitudinal histories. Simulations can test warnings for deliberately detectable support failures, but no estimator can be required to detect every nonidentifiable target from the observed distribution alone. No package capability claim is present.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Flexible learners can reduce nuisance-model approximation error but cannot repair nonidentification. Existing support and overlap diagnostics can flag particular forms of extrapolation, but they are definition- and model-dependent and cannot certify sequential exchangeability, positivity, or identification in general, especially with high-dimensional treatment histories.

opinions.rationale: Inverted search did not find a standard that closes this gap. Feuerriegel et al. (Nat Med 2024) restate that causal ML requires the same identification assumptions as classical methods and does not identify contrasts the data cannot support; that is prior art for the claim, not a solution. Hill and Su (Ann Appl Stat 2013) and Nethery et al. (Ann Appl Stat 2019) give BART-centered common-support diagnostics and nonoverlap-aware estimation, and propensity-score density/trim diagnostics remain routine for low-dimensional scores. Those tools do not constitute a diagnostic in common use that flags, for a general flexible nuisance (including neural nets) and for the same high-dimensional conditioning sets the nuisance uses, which predictions are interpolation versus extrapolation. Package activity in TrialEmulation, gfoRmula, lmtp, WeightIt, and related tools still emphasizes IPW weight extremity and classical overlap plots rather than per-prediction support maps for flexible outcome models. Failure-awareness scoring against deliberately non-identifiable simulations is not an established methods-comparison standard. The problem remains open as stated for applied flexible nuisance work; the caveat is that specialized support diagnostics for some nonparametric models already exist and should be named rather than implied to be nonexistent.

The claim correctly identifies that identification is a property of data and assumptions, not the estimator, and that flexible models can disguise extrapolation. The reason given for it being open (lack of common diagnostics for high-dimensional extrapolation) logically supports the claim. The claim is pitched at the right level of generality and correctly frames the issue as a current practice gap rather than a structural impossibility.

title: Automated protocol translation can change the estimand while producing valid code
statement: Systems now translate trial descriptions into cohort definitions or analysis code, and natural language processing extracts eligibility information from unstructured notes. The failure mode of these systems is not that they crash. It is that they silently substitute a different estimand: mistranslating a temporal condition, resolving an ambiguous eligibility phrase to the wrong operationalization, or emitting code that is syntactically valid and causally invalid. None of these failures is visible in the output, which is a working pipeline returning a plausible number. What is missing is a validation regime that treats generated code as an untrusted artifact rather than as a productivity gain.
why_open: Temporal logic is where these systems fail and where testing is hardest: the difference between treatment before eligibility assessment and treatment after it is one word in the specification and one join condition in the code, and both readings execute. There is no reference answer to test against, because the correct cohort is precisely what the pipeline was built to produce. Evaluating on downstream effect estimates is circular, since a wrong cohort with a plausible effect passes.

proposed_direction: Treat automation as a constrained compiler with three stages: a human-authored causal specification, a typed intermediate representation, and data-source-specific code generated from it. Require unit tests over synthetic test patients constructed so that each temporal condition has a patient that distinguishes the correct reading from the plausible wrong one, plus temporal-logic validation of the intermediate representation. Require dual human sign-off on the specification and on the generated cohort counts, and publish both, so the artifact under review is the specification rather than the number.
severity: These systems scale one analyst's error to every study that uses them.

opinions.rationale: Executable code can silently change eligibility, time zero, assignment, follow-up, or the resulting estimand, so the core risk is real. However, it is false that such errors are necessarily invisible or that no reference answer can exist. Independently authored specifications, expert-labeled records, hand-coded reference implementations, differential testing, and synthetic boundary-case patients can provide component-level or end-to-end reference answers. The report's own proposed synthetic-patient tests contradict the categorical no-reference-answer claim. Agreement of a downstream effect estimate is insufficient evidence of semantic correctness, but evaluating against an external randomized benchmark is not literally circular. Typed intermediate representations and temporal tests reduce risk without proving semantic equivalence for every real-world mapping. No package capability claim is present.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Automated protocol translation can produce validly executing code that implements a different estimand. Full gold-standard cohorts may be unavailable for some real datasets, but semantic fidelity can still be tested against independently specified protocols, expert annotations, reference implementations, and synthetic temporal boundary cases; downstream numerical plausibility alone does not validate the translation.

opinions.rationale: Kim et al. (JAMIA Open 2026; THESEUS) and Wang et al. (npj Digit Med 2026) build or specify automated protocol-to-code and operational EHR mappings; they are the systems whose silent estimand-shift risk the problem names, not fixes of that risk. Lee et al. (JMIR Med Inform 2025) validate LLM-generated trial-criteria queries for functional correctness, which is partial operational testing but not temporal-logic unit tests that distinguish treatment-before versus treatment-after eligibility. Girshovitz, Zeltzer, and Gilad-Bachrach (arXiv:2607.21173, 2026) propose ARA: structured protocol intermediate form, SCM synthetic failure scenarios, and adversarial validation so that silent success is replaced by visible protocol or diagnostic failure. That is closely aligned with the report direction, yet it is a proposal with a small econometric-style benchmark; it does not establish a standard validation regime for TTE automation, dual human sign-off on specification and cohort counts, or synthetic patients that isolate each temporal join. Guidance (TARGET 2025 reporting; FDA/EMA RWE documents) addresses transparency of human-designed emulations, not untrusted machine-generated code. No CRAN or GitHub merge was found that ships a constrained TTE compiler with temporal unit tests. Silent estimand substitution under syntactically valid pipelines remains open.

The claim is internally consistent and correctly identifies the silent estimand substitution as a structural risk in automated translation. The reasons given for it being open (lack of reference answers, circularity of downstream evaluation) strongly support the claim. The scope is appropriate and the severity is proportionate to the cost of a wrong estimand.

title: Learned embeddings from clinical text can carry post-treatment information into a baseline adjustment set
statement: Notes, imaging and device data capture severity, treatment rationale and outcomes that structured fields miss, and natural language processing has been proposed for eligibility extraction and phenotyping on that basis. The risk is specific: a learned representation of a clinical note is a dense summary of everything in the note, which can include post-treatment information, the identity of the site, the behavior of the treating clinician and protected characteristics. Adjusting for such a representation is adjusting for an object whose causal role is unknown and probably mixed, and the usual justification, that more information reduces confounding, does not hold when part of that information is a descendant of treatment.
why_open: The causal role of an embedding dimension is not interpretable, so the standard remedy of inspecting the adjustment set does not apply. Temporal leakage is easy to introduce and hard to detect, because a note timestamped before treatment can still describe a treatment decision already made. Restricting to pre-assignment text limits the leak but does not eliminate it, and no test distinguishes a representation that encodes prognosis from one that encodes the treatment that was about to be given.

prior_work.cite: Wang, et al. An operational target trial emulation framework for causal inference using electronic health records. npj Digit Med 2026
prior_work.what_it_does: Proposes natural language processing for eligibility extraction and phenotyping within an emulation framework.

prior_work.what_it_does: Sets the boundary between predictive performance and causal validity that high-dimensional adjustment repeatedly crosses.

proposed_direction: Use temporally locked encoders trained only on pre-assignment text, and audit the resulting representations for treatment leakage by testing whether the embedding predicts the assigned treatment better than the structured pre-assignment covariates do. Prefer interpretable proxy sets, or an explicit proximal role in which the proxy's function is stated, over indiscriminate adjustment for a high-dimensional representation. Report what the embedding was allowed to see, in dates rather than in prose, because that is the claim on which its validity rests.
severity: Text-derived adjustment is being adopted quickly and the failure mode improves apparent balance while adding bias.

opinions.rationale: A search for treatment leakage, temporal locking or auditing of learned representations used as adjustment sets returned nothing in the screened corpus. The claim is therefore unrefuted and weakly evidenced: the corpus is built from target trial and g-method phrases, and work on representation leakage would most likely appear in machine learning venues that none of the eight phrases reaches. The vote is open at the confidence ceiling this project sets for searched-and-found-nothing.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: No published emulation audits a text-derived representation used for adjustment for post-treatment information, and no convention states what window of text an encoder was permitted to see.

opinions.rationale: An embedding derived from content observed after treatment assignment or after the clinical treatment decision can encode descendants of treatment and make baseline adjustment invalid. The risk is conditional on the source content and causal timing, not on representation learning or opacity by itself. A deterministic embedding of genuinely baseline variables remains baseline, and site or protected characteristics are not automatically invalid adjustment variables. Individual embedding dimensions need not be causally interpretable if the provenance and causal roles of their inputs are defensible. The proposed treatment-prediction test is not a valid leakage diagnostic: stronger prediction of assigned treatment can arise from additional legitimate confounder information, instruments, or actual leakage, and the test cannot distinguish these explanations. Likewise, merely declaring an embedding a proximal proxy is insufficient without valid proxy roles and the associated identifying conditions. No package capability claim is present.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Embeddings whose input window is not demonstrably prior to treatment assignment and the underlying treatment decision can carry post-treatment or decision-related information into a nominal baseline adjustment set. Validity therefore requires auditable content provenance and causal timing. Treatment predictiveness alone neither establishes nor rules out leakage, and a proximal interpretation requires explicit proxy roles and additional identification conditions.

opinions.rationale: The report frames embedding adjustment as an open risk without naming the literature that already defines and partially remediates it. Daoud, Jerzak, and Johansson (NAACL 2022) formalize treatment leakage when text is used as a confounder proxy, including leakage from pre-assignment documents that anticipate treatment. Daoud, Johansson, and Jerzak (arXiv:2601.02400, late 2025/2026) add formal definitions, four distillation methods (similarity passage removal, distant-supervision passage classification, salient-feature removal, iterative nullspace projection), and simulation plus empirical sensitivity analysis; they explicitly address the paradox that pre-timestamped text can still encode treatment. That is real prior art for detection and mitigation, not mere restatement. Residual openness remains for clinical TTE: methods are not standard in EHR phenotyping pipelines; Wang et al. (2026) still promote NLP for eligibility without a required leakage audit; temporal locking plus formal comparison of embedding-versus-structured treatment prediction is recommended in the agenda and only partially operationalized outside medicine. Sensitivity and distillation quantify or reduce leakage; they do not make an embedding's causal role fully interpretable dimension-by-dimension. The problem is therefore partially solved in the text-as-confounder literature and still under-adopted in clinical emulation practice.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Clinical-note and other high-dimensional embeddings used as baseline covariates can encode treatment-related content even when timestamps precede assignment; formal treatment-leakage methods and text distillation exist, but they are not yet standard practice in target trial emulations, and no routine test fully certifies that an embedding encodes only pre-treatment prognosis.

title: Phenotypes enter emulations as error-free binary variables
statement: Prescriptions differ from dispensings and dispensings differ from ingestion; diagnostic codes differ from clinical events; death and care received outside the system may be incompletely captured. Methods for outcome misclassification in electronic health records increasingly use validation samples and probabilistic phenotypes. Emulation pipelines almost universally do not: a phenotype is thresholded to a binary variable at the start and treated as truth thereafter. Differential misclassification then interacts with weighting and with time-varying confounding in ways that are not intuitive, because an error in the exposure at one time propagates into the weights at every later time, and no standard analysis propagates the phenotype uncertainty at all.
why_open: The interaction is genuinely nonlinear: misclassification in a time-varying confounder both biases the weight and changes which patients are censored, so the bias does not decompose into a measurement part and a confounding part. Validation samples that would calibrate the phenotype are usually convenience samples from one site, and transporting a sensitivity and specificity across sites is itself an untested transport claim. Propagating uncertainty end to end also requires the whole pipeline to accept probabilistic inputs, which most implementations cannot.

Simulate sensitivity and specificity from 0.70 to 0.99 with differential misclassification odds ratios from 1 to 4, and report the bias in the estimated regime effect rather than in the phenotype, since the phenotype's accuracy is not what the study claims. Establish how large a validation sample has to be before the correction is worth its variance cost.
severity: Every record-based emulation rests on phenotypes and almost none of them carry their error forward.

Design-bias reviews name outcome misclassification among the biases to avoid without supplying the propagation. The entry's specific claim, that the interaction between differential misclassification, weighting and time-varying confounding is not handled, is consistent with what the corpus shows.

resolving_work.title: Identifying and avoiding design related biases in observational studies using the target trial framework
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Enumerates design-related biases including measurement, showing the problem is recognized within the framework without being handled quantitatively.

opinions.rationale: The underlying joint longitudinal measurement-error problem is real, but several assertions are too categorical. Prescribing, dispensing, and ingestion are distinct variables; their difference is misclassification only when the estimand targets one but the protocol measures another. In a cumulative inverse-probability weight, an erroneous treatment factor at time s remains in later cumulative products for a clone still at risk, but a clone artificially censored at s has no later weights. Mismeasurement of a time-varying confounder changes artificial-censoring membership only when that variable determines the dynamic strategy, eligibility, or censoring rule; under a static sustained strategy it can distort nuisance models without changing who is censored. The resulting biases can interact, but the defensible claim is that no unique identified additive measurement-versus-confounding decomposition generally exists without additional assumptions, not that no decomposition is possible. End-to-end propagation also does not require every estimator to accept soft inputs natively: multiple imputation, posterior draws, or a whole-pipeline bootstrap can wrap deterministic estimators. No package is named, so the claims about 'almost universally,' 'no standard analysis,' and 'most implementations' cannot be established from package ground truth. TrialEmulation 0.0.4.11 confirms one indicator-based implementation, not the asserted prevalence. The narrowed problem remains open, while uniformly assigning very-high severity is unjustified because importance depends on the estimand, error mechanism, validation information, and decision sensitivity.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: When a target trial's treatment, time-varying confounder, eligibility criterion, or outcome is a latent clinical state but the emulation analyzes an error-prone thresholded proxy as fixed, differential longitudinal misclassification can jointly distort adherence decisions, treatment or censoring weights, and the regime-effect estimate. For clones remaining at risk, an erroneous weight factor persists in subsequent cumulative weights; artificial-censoring membership changes only when the mismeasured variable enters the strategy, eligibility, or censoring rule. Without validation information and assumptions identifying and transporting a joint measurement model, a unique separation of measurement and confounding bias is generally unavailable. Native probabilistic-input support would be useful, but deterministic pipelines can instead be embedded within multiple-imputation, posterior-draw, or bootstrap procedures.

counter_evidence.quote: sw_data[(first == FALSE & am_1 != treatment), switch := 1]

opinions.rationale:
Inverted prior: searched for an end-to-end solution that lets sustained-strategy or time-varying TTE pipelines take probabilistic (non-thresholded) treatment, confounder, and outcome phenotypes and propagate differential misclassification through weights and censoring into the regime-effect interval. Nothing retrieved closes that full claim.

Own citations first. Wang et al. (npj Digit Med 2026; 10.1038/s41746-026-02563-z) is an operational TTE framework paper. Available text describes validation samples and probabilistic or uncertainty-aware outcome models as tools that can account for measurement error, and separately reviews g-methods for sustained strategies. It does not deliver a validated pipeline that accepts probabilistic treatment and outcome nodes end to end, nor simulations of regime-effect bias under differential time-varying misclassification. Description of existing pieces is not resolution. Benz et al. (Am J Epidemiol 2025; 10.1093/aje/kwae471; arXiv:2406.16830) targets selection bias from missing eligibility criteria via IPW under an MAR-type assumption for eligibility ascertainment. It is a useful template for validation-anchored IPW on one protocol component; it is not phenotype measurement-error correction for time-varying exposure or confounders.

Component prior art (does not close the stated gap). Hubbard, Tong, Duan, Chen (Epidemiology 2020; 10.1097/EDE.0000000000001193) give a hand-computable bias correction for continuous EHR probabilistic outcome phenotypes in association studies. Scope is outcome misclassification and association parameters, not time-varying treatment weights or sustained regimes. Edwards et al. (Am J Epidemiol 2018; 10.1093/aje/kwy028) fold sensitivity analysis for cause-of-death misclassification into the parametric g-formula; that is quantitative bias analysis, not identification with validation-anchored probabilistic nodes. Edwards et al. (RIME; PubMed 31971584, 2020) reparameterize imputation for exposure misclassification with validation data and illustrate combination with IPW for hazard ratios and risks: point-exposure misclassification with IPW, not full longitudinal differential error in exposure, confounders, and outcomes under dynamic or sustained strategies. Nab et al. (Epidemiology 2020) quantify bias from a misclassified confounder in MSM-IPW; characterization and QBA, not a solved TTE pipeline. Lu et al. (J Biomed Inform 2024; 10.1016/j.jbi.2024.104690) leverage multiple error-prone algorithm phenotypes plus a small validation set for risk-factor associations: again association, not TTE g-methods.

Material that strengthens openness. Ross, Cole, et al. (Epidemiology 2024; 35(2):196–207) document challenges of transporting measurement-error parameters (sensitivity, specificity, and related bias parameters) from external validation data: this supports the report’s claim that Se/Sp transport across sites is itself an untested or fragile transport claim, not a solved step.

Software (CRAN/GitHub scan). TrialEmulation, gfoRmula, gfoRmulaICE, lmtp, ltmle, survtmle, WeightIt, MatchIt, cobalt, ipw, adjustedCurves, riskRegression, and related Python stacks (zEpid, causallib, lifelines, scikit-survival) remain binary or continuous node pipelines for treatment and outcome after analyst thresholding. CRAN’s causal-inference task view points measurement-error tooling to sensitivity packages (e.g., episensr, EValue), not first-class probabilistic phenotype inputs inside sequential TTE or g-formula estimation. No merged PR or release note retrieved that closes end-to-end phenotype uncertainty in these packages through 2025–2026.

Queries run (representative): Wang operational TTE DOI and Nature page/PDF; Benz kwae471/arXiv; “probabilistic phenotype” + causal/IPTW/g-formula/lmtp/ltmle/TTE 2023–2026; measurement error misclassification + MSM-IPW / g-formula / time-varying / sustained strategy; Hubbard probabilistic phenotypes; Edwards RIME and g-formula misclassification; Ross transporting measurement error; CRAN/GitHub TrialEmulation gfoRmula lmtp measurement error; TARGET/ENCePP/FDA RWE measurement error guidance cross-check. Journals and preprint venues searched via web for 2024–2026 hits on those terms.

Caveat on support: the entry is faithful that standard TTE pipelines threshold phenotypes and that the nonlinear interaction of differential time-varying misclassification with weighting and censoring is not handled end to end. It would be overstated only if read as “no methods exist for any piece of phenotype error.” Pieces exist (outcome probabilistic correction in associations; exposure misclassification with IPW; g-formula outcome SA; transport problems formalized). None of those pieces, alone or as packaged software, solves the problem as stated for sustained-strategy emulation with uncertainty carried to the final interval.

The statement correctly identifies a methodological gap in target trial emulation using EHR data.
